flashcards.question: What is ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOR (OB) and its GOAL?
flashcards.answer:
BEHAVIOR = simply the things people do and say (our actions).
OB = the study of ACTIONS that affect performance in the workplace.

The goal of OB theorists is to UNDERSTAND, EXPLAIN, PREDICT and INFLUENCE behavior to improve performance.
flashcards.explanation: OB is about 'reading people'; interpersonal skills are key to success.

flashcards.question: What are the FOUNDATIONS of individual behavior?
flashcards.answer:
Our thoughts, self-confidence, self-esteem, personality, perception, and attitudes.

These foundations are NOT observable — you can only observe actions and try to explain/predict behavior from your understanding of the foundations.
flashcards.explanation: It's about reading people; OB skills help build and maintain good relationships.

flashcards.question: SELF-ESTEEM vs SELF-CONFIDENCE vs SELF-DOUBT?
flashcards.answer:
• SELF-ESTEEM — your overall view of yourself (like/dislike yourself). Not innate; shaped by experience and thoughts.
• SELF-CONFIDENCE — believing you can do a SPECIFIC task (also called self-efficacy/self-concept); an 'I can do this' attitude.
• SELF-DOUBT — negative thoughts that hold us back; leads to fear of rejection/failure/risk.
flashcards.explanation: Improve them through positive SELF-TALK and visualizing success.

flashcards.question: How do THOUGHTS, optimism and gratitude affect behavior?
flashcards.answer:
Thoughts cause our feelings, behavior and performance ('what you think is what you get').
• OPTIMISM — believing things will go well; less stress, happier, higher performance than pessimists.
• GRATITUDE — grateful people are happier, healthier, less stressed.
• SELF-TALK — comments/reminders/advice you give yourself ('no stinking thinking').
flashcards.explanation: As Henry Ford said: whether you think you'll succeed or fail, you're right.

flashcards.question: What is PERSONALITY, and the LOCUS OF CONTROL trait?
flashcards.answer:
PERSONALITY = a combination of behavioral, mental and emotional traits that define an individual; a primary influence on how we behave.

LOCUS OF CONTROL lies on a continuum:
• EXTERNALIZERS — believe they have no control over their fate.
• INTERNALIZERS — believe they control their fate; their behavior directly affects performance → higher self-esteem, self-confidence, and performance.
flashcards.explanation: Internalizers have been shown to have higher levels of performance.

flashcards.question: RISK PROPENSITY, entrepreneurial types and MACHIAVELLIANISM?
flashcards.answer:
• RISK PROPENSITY — continuum from risk taking to risk avoiding; entrepreneurs are risk takers.
• ENTREPRENEURIAL TYPES — hustlers, innovators, machines, prodigies, visionaries.
• MACHIAVELLIANISM — a trait based on the belief that the ends justify the means and power should be used to reach desired ends. Also called NARCISSIST — manipulate others for selfish gain; lack empathy.
flashcards.explanation: Risk-avoiding managers often go out of business by not keeping up with change.

flashcards.question: What are the BIG FIVE personality dimensions (OCEAN)?
flashcards.answer:
The Five-Factor Model — abbreviated OCEAN:
• OPENNESS — willing to try new things (good for creative jobs).
• CONSCIENTIOUSNESS — responsible, dependable, hardworking (overall best predictor of job success).
• EXTRAVERSION — social, talkative, assertive (good for sales/leadership); middle = 'ambivert'.
• AGREEABLENESS — cooperative, easy to work with (good for teamwork).
• NEUROTICISM / EMOTIONALISM — continuum of emotional stability vs instability.
flashcards.explanation: Emotional intelligence (EI) describes people with good interpersonal skills.

learn.title: Organizational Behavior
learn.content:
What is OB?

The study of actions that affect performance at work. Goal: understand → explain → predict → influence behavior.

Foundations of behavior

  • Self-esteem (overall view) · self-confidence/self-efficacy (a task) · self-doubt
  • Thoughts · optimism · gratitude · positive self-talk + visualization

Personality

  • Locus of control: internalizers (control fate, higher performance) vs externalizers
  • Risk propensity · entrepreneurial types · Machiavellianism (narcissism)
  • Big Five (OCEAN): Openness · Conscientiousness · Extraversion · Agreeableness · Neuroticism

flashcards.question: What is MOTIVATION, and the PERFORMANCE FORMULA?
flashcards.answer:
MOTIVATION = the willingness to achieve organizational objectives or to go above and beyond (organizational citizenship behavior, OCB; 'employee engagement').

PERFORMANCE FORMULA: performance = ability × motivation × resources.

For maximum performance, ALL THREE factors must be high (it's multiplicative — a zero in any factor kills performance).
flashcards.explanation: Effort has three parts: initiation, direction, and persistence.

flashcards.question: What is the MOTIVATION PROCESS?
flashcards.answer:
Employees go from NEED → MOTIVE → BEHAVIOR → CONSEQUENCE → SATISFACTION or DISSATISFACTION.

Example: thirsty (need) → desire a drink (motive) → get a drink (behavior) → quench thirst (consequence/satisfaction). Satisfaction is short-lived, so it's a FEEDBACK LOOP.
flashcards.explanation: You can't observe motives, only behavior — infer motive via the attribution process.

flashcards.question: Compare the three CLASSES of motivation theories.
flashcards.answer:
1. CONTENT theories — identify and understand employees' NEEDS (what motivates).
2. PROCESS theories — explain HOW and WHY employees choose behaviors to satisfy needs.
3. REINFORCEMENT theory — uses CONSEQUENCES of behavior; no need to identify needs.
flashcards.explanation: There is no single universally accepted theory of how to motivate people.

flashcards.question: What are the four CONTENT motivation theories?
flashcards.answer:
1. MASLOW's HIERARCHY OF NEEDS — 5 levels: physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualization.
2. ALDERFER's ERG — simplifies to 3: Existence, Relatedness, Growth (more than one can be active).
3. HERZBERG's TWO-FACTOR — MAINTENANCE factors (extrinsic; prevent dissatisfaction) vs MOTIVATORS (intrinsic; create satisfaction).
4. McCLELLAND's ACQUIRED NEEDS — achievement, power, affiliation (learned; one is dominant).
flashcards.explanation: Managers tend to have high need for Power, then Achievement, and low Affiliation.

flashcards.question: Explain HERZBERG'S two-factor theory.
flashcards.answer:
Employees are motivated by MOTIVATORS, not maintenance factors.
• MAINTENANCE (hygiene) factors — extrinsic (pay, conditions, security). Continuum: 'not dissatisfied ↔ dissatisfied'. Fixing them removes dissatisfaction but doesn't motivate.
• MOTIVATORS — intrinsic, from the work itself (achievement, recognition, growth). Continuum: 'satisfied ↔ not satisfied'.
flashcards.explanation: Example: a pay raise stops dissatisfaction, but soon the cycle repeats — pay is a maintenance factor.

flashcards.question: What are the three PROCESS motivation theories?
flashcards.answer:
1. EQUITY theory (J. S. Adams) — motivated when perceived INPUTS = OUTPUTS compared to relevant others; perceived unfairness changes behavior.
2. GOAL-SETTING theory — achievable but DIFFICULT, specific goals motivate ('stretch goals').
3. EXPECTANCY theory (Vroom) — motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence.
flashcards.explanation: Expectancy = can I do it?; instrumentality = will performance lead to the reward?; valence = do I value the reward?

flashcards.question: What is REINFORCEMENT theory and its 4 types?
flashcards.answer:
Consequences of behavior motivate employees to behave in predetermined ways. Four types:
1. POSITIVE — offer an attractive consequence (reward) → encourages behavior.
2. AVOIDANCE (negative reinforcement) — behavior prevents a negative consequence.
3. PUNISHMENT — apply a negative consequence to DECREASE undesirable behavior.
4. EXTINCTION — WITHHOLD reinforcement to reduce/eliminate a behavior.
flashcards.explanation: Positive (reward) & avoidance encourage desired behavior; positive reinforcement generally works better than punishment.

learn.title: Motivating for High Performance
learn.content:
The basics

performance = ability × motivation × resources  (all three must be high)
process: NEED → MOTIVE → BEHAVIOR → CONSEQUENCE → (dis)SATISFACTION

Three classes of theory

  • Content (needs): Maslow hierarchy · Alderfer ERG · Herzberg two-factor · McClelland acquired needs
  • Process (how/why): equity · goal-setting (stretch goals) · expectancy (E × I × V)
  • Reinforcement (consequences): positive · avoidance · punishment · extinction

Herzberg: maintenance factors only stop dissatisfaction; motivators (the work itself) create real motivation. Expectancy: can I do it? × will it pay off? × do I value it?

flashcards.question: What is LEADERSHIP, and why does TRUST matter?
flashcards.answer:
LEADERSHIP = the process of INFLUENCING employees to work toward achieving objectives.

Good relationships are based on TRUST. A survey found 74% of ENGAGED employees trust their manager, while only 14% don't trust their boss. People won't go 'above and beyond' for a boss they don't trust — and managers must also be able to trust employees.
flashcards.explanation: Trustworthiness is based on (at least) four dimensions.

flashcards.question: How do LEADERS differ from MANAGERS?
flashcards.answer:
Management gives POSITION power and is broader in scope; leadership is the ability to INFLUENCE others.

• A manager can hold the position WITHOUT being a true leader (no trust/influence).
• There are good leaders who are NOT managers (informal/peer leaders).

So leadership doesn't require a title — you can be an informal leader (e.g. Steve Jobs = great leader but not a great manager; Tim Cook = both).
flashcards.explanation: Leadership is critical to management success.

flashcards.question: What are the FOUR classifications of leadership THEORIES?
flashcards.answer:
All have the same goal (what makes an effective leader), but different focus:
1. TRAIT theory — leaders' characteristics/traits.
2. BEHAVIORAL theory — leaders' styles/behavior.
3. SITUATIONAL (contingency) theory — matching style to the situation.
4. CONTEMPORARY/integrative — visionary, charismatic, transformational, etc.
flashcards.explanation: Trait theory began with the assumption that leaders are born, not made.

flashcards.question: What are the BEHAVIORAL leadership styles (Lewin's three)?
flashcards.answer:
Kurt Lewin (University of Iowa) identified three basic styles:
• AUTOCRATIC (≈ Theory X) — leader makes decisions, tells employees what to do.
• DEMOCRATIC (≈ Theory Y) — leader includes employees in decisions.
• LAISSEZ-FAIRE — a 'leave-employees-alone' hands-off approach.
flashcards.explanation: Two-dimensional styles combine STRUCTURING (task) and CONSIDERATION (relationships).

flashcards.question: What is the LEADERSHIP GRID and its 5 styles?
flashcards.answer:
Measures concern for PRODUCTION and concern for PEOPLE on a 1–9 scale. Five styles:
• (1,1) IMPOVERISHED — low concern for both.
• (9,1) AUTHORITY-COMPLIANCE — high production, low people.
• (1,9) COUNTRY CLUB — high people, low production.
• (5,5) MIDDLE-OF-THE-ROAD — balanced medium concern.
• (9,9) TEAM — high concern for both (the ideal).
flashcards.explanation: The ideal style incorporates high concern for both production and people.

flashcards.question: What is SITUATIONAL (contingency) leadership?
flashcards.answer:
Attempts to determine the appropriate leadership style for a PARTICULAR situation — how leaders behave is CONTINGENT on the situation. No single style fits all situations.

The LEADERSHIP CONTINUUM MODEL (Tannenbaum & Schmidt) chooses among 7 styles from AUTOCRATIC (boss-centered) to PARTICIPATIVE (employee-centered), considering: the leader's preferred style, the followers' preferred style, and the situation.
flashcards.explanation: Also called contingency theory because behavior is contingent on the situation.

flashcards.question: Name the CONTEMPORARY leadership styles.
flashcards.answer:
• VISIONARY — creates an image of the organization's FUTURE (e.g. Musk → Mars).
• CHARISMATIC — inspires loyalty, enthusiasm via confident personal traits.
• TRANSFORMATIONAL — brings continuous learning, innovation and CHANGE; gets followers to transcend self-interest (e.g. Bezos).
• TRANSACTIONAL — based on social EXCHANGE ('do this work and I'll reward you'); promotes stability.
• AUTHENTIC — open, honest, trusting relationships; leads by example.
flashcards.explanation: Transformational leaders are especially needed in growth firms in dynamic environments.

learn.title: Leading With Influence
learn.content:
Leadership = influence

The process of influencing employees toward objectives. Built on trust. A manager can hold the position without being a true leader; leaders can exist without a title.

Four theory classifications

  1. Trait — born vs made
  2. Behavioral — Lewin (autocratic/democratic/laissez-faire); two-dimensional (structuring × consideration); Leadership Grid (1,1 / 9,1 / 1,9 / 5,5 / 9,9 team)
  3. Situational/contingency — Tannenbaum & Schmidt continuum (7 styles, boss → employee centered)
  4. Contemporary — visionary · charismatic · transformational · transactional · authentic

Transformational (change, transcend self-interest) vs transactional (exchange, stability). Visionary shapes the future; authentic leads by example.

flashcards.question: What is CONTROLLING, and the types of ORGANIZATIONAL SYSTEMS control?
flashcards.answer:
CONTROLLING = monitoring progress and taking corrective action to ensure objectives are achieved ('you can't manage what you don't measure').

Controls in the systems process:
• PRELIMINARY (feedforward) — anticipate & PREVENT problems (inputs).
• CONCURRENT — ensure standards are met DURING transformation.
• REWORK — fix a faulty OUTPUT.
• DAMAGE control — minimize negative impact on customers (e.g. warranties).
• FEEDBACK — use customer input for continuous improvement.
flashcards.explanation: Preliminary control = planning & organizing; it's better to prevent than to fix.

flashcards.question: What are the 4 STEPS of the CONTROL SYSTEMS PROCESS?
flashcards.answer:
1. SET objectives and standards.
2. MEASURE performance.
3. COMPARE performance to standards (a performance/variance report).
4. CORRECT or REINFORCE (fix it if off; reinforce if on track).

Followed at both organizational and functional-area levels.
flashcards.explanation: When variances are significant, they must be explained.

flashcards.question: What 5 AREAS must complete STANDARDS cover?
flashcards.answer:
Standards measure performance in:
1. QUANTITY (how many?)
2. QUALITY (how well?)
3. TIME (when / how fast?)
4. COST (how much should it cost?)
5. BEHAVIOR (what to do / not do; ethics)

Incomplete standards make employees 'game' the system (e.g. quantity-only → ignore quality).
flashcards.explanation: Critical success factors (CSFs) = the few most important areas to control.

flashcards.question: What are the 3 frequencies and 10 METHODS of control?
flashcards.answer:
• CONSTANT (continuous): self-control, clan control, standing plans.
• PERIODIC (regular/fixed): regular meetings & reports, budgets, audits.
• OCCASIONAL (sporadic): observation, the exception principle, special reports, project controls.
flashcards.explanation: Clan control relies on culture/norms and peer pressure; the exception principle leaves control to employees unless a problem occurs.

flashcards.question: What is the MASTER BUDGETING process (3 steps)?
flashcards.answer:
A BUDGET = a planned quantitative allocation of resources (not just money). Steps:
1. OPERATING budgets — REVENUE budget (forecast income) + EXPENSE budget (forecast spending).
2. CAPITAL EXPENDITURES budget — all planned major ASSET investments (land, buildings, equipment).
3. FINANCIAL budgets — budgeted (pro forma) income statement, balance sheet, cash flow.
flashcards.explanation: Budgeting needs PLANNING skills, not math/accounting skills; a feedback loop allows revisions.

flashcards.question: What are the THREE primary FINANCIAL STATEMENTS?
flashcards.answer:
1. INCOME STATEMENT — presents revenue, expenses and the PROFIT or LOSS for a period.
2. BALANCE SHEET — presents ASSETS = LIABILITIES + owners'/stockholders' EQUITY (it must balance at a point in time).
3. CASH FLOW STATEMENT — cash receipts and payments (operating + financial activities).

PROFIT MARGIN = net profit ÷ revenue. Pro forma = projected; actual statements report the past.
flashcards.explanation: You can have high revenues yet low/no profit — watch the profit margin.

flashcards.question: BONDS vs STOCK for raising money?
flashcards.answer:
Both raise capital but differ as DEBT vs EQUITY:
• BONDS (debt) — the firm must REPAY bondholders + interest; no ownership given away; lower risk, lower return.
• STOCK (equity) — the firm NEVER repays; stockholders become PART OWNERS; the firm only gets money at the initial public offering (IPO). Give away too much and you can lose control.
flashcards.explanation: Selling bonds/stock doesn't affect the income statement, but it does affect the balance sheet & cash flow.

flashcards.question: What are COACHING, COUNSELING and DISCIPLINE?
flashcards.answer:
• COACHING — giving MOTIVATIONAL feedback to maintain/improve performance.
• MANAGEMENT COUNSELING — giving feedback so employees realize a problem affects their job, then referring them to the employee assistance program (NOT psychotherapy).
• DISCIPLINE — corrective action to get employees to meet standards/standing plans; objective is to CHANGE behavior (deviance = negative voluntary behavior).
flashcards.explanation: Coaching/counseling come first; discipline follows if an employee won't change or breaks a rule.

learn.title: Managing Control Systems, Finances & People
learn.content:
Controlling = monitor + correct

SYSTEMS CONTROLS: preliminary (inputs) → concurrent (process) → rework (outputs) → damage → feedback
PROCESS: set standards → measure → compare → correct/reinforce

Standards & frequency

  • 5 standard areas: quantity · quality · time · cost · behavior (+ critical success factors)
  • Constant: self · clan · standing plans · Periodic: meetings · budgets · audits · Occasional: observation · exception principle · special reports · project

Finances & people

  • Master budget: operating (revenue + expense) → capital expenditures → financial (pro forma)
  • Statements: income statement · balance sheet (A = L + E) · cash flow; profit margin = net profit ÷ revenue
  • Raising money: bonds (debt, repay + interest) vs stock (equity, ownership, IPO)
  • People: coaching → counseling → discipline (change behavior); handling complaints
